quote: The claimant must have an accurate model of the situation somewhere in their mind, because they can anticipate, in advance, exactly which experimental results they’ll need to excuse.
content: In the parable, every excuse comes before the test is run, and every one is correct. The claimant says the dragon is inaudible before anyone listens, and permeable to flour before the flour is thrown. A generator of excuses with no model behind it would sometimes let a test go ahead and be caught. This one never does, and that is the evidence of an accurate model somewhere. Kunda's motivated reasoner works under exactly this constraint: the justifications have to be ones that would persuade "a dispassionate observer," so the reasoner must know which conclusions the evidence will not support (Kunda 1990). Motivated reasoning that knows where the evidence lies is the essay's hidden model under another name.

quote: Some philosophers have been much confused by such scenarios
content: The literature the note lists reaches the essay's thesis independently, and mostly later. Sperber's reflective beliefs, Gendler's aliefs and Van Leeuwen's religious credences all make the essay's claim: a mind holds several kinds of belief-like state, and the dragon-claimant's avowal is not the state that guides his expectations (Van Leeuwen 2014). Gendler and Van Leeuwen published after the essay. The "confused" philosophers are those who ask whether the claimant "really" believes, as though there were a single answer. That question is still being asked, which is why Van Leeuwen's paper needed writing.

quote: not unless they are unusually capable of acknowledging their own lack of virtue
content: The note's examples bear the clause out. "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief" opens by avowing belief and treats the doubt as a defect to be cured. That is belief in belief speaking; it is not "I do not believe, but I believe I ought to." Pascal's reader, told to act as if he believed until belief follows, knows he does not yet believe, and Pascal treats him as a special case to be argued with. Luhrmann's evangelicals describe the work of believing, but they describe it as learning to hear God, not as holding a belief they lack (Luhrmann 2012, When God Talks Back, book, no DOI). An explicit, first-person "I only believe in belief" is still rare, as the essay says.

quote: you may remember a time period when you first began to doubt Santa Claus’s existence, but you still believed that you were supposed to believe in Santa Claus, so you tried to deny the doubts
content: The essay's sentence begins "Depending on how your childhood went" and does not claim a developmental universal. The studies cited describe the typical child. The essay describes one path through the distribution and invites readers to recognize it. The parental-promotion finding predicts that path: where adults press the belief hardest, the child has the most reason to feel it must be kept after doubts arrive (Goldstein & Woolley 2016, Cognitive Development). That most children take the discovery well is compatible with a period of trying to go on believing. A happy ending says nothing about whether the doubts were denied first.

quote: the dragon-claimant anticipates as if there is no dragon in their garage, and makes excuses as if they believed in the belief
content: Coexistence is not the symptom the essay names. Legare's subjects hold natural and supernatural accounts of the same event and use each where it fits, and none of them rules out a test in advance (Legare et al. 2012). The "something much worse" is a specific configuration: the believer anticipates as if there were no dragon and produces excuses ahead of time to protect the avowal. The essay's earlier paragraphs say plainly that having several types of belief is normal: "Real minds are more tangled than that." Fable has matched the essay's general claim against its diagnosis of one pathology within it.
